Pandémie ou pas, la communauté kanien’ke: Pandemic or not, the Kanien’kehá:ka (Mohawk) community is doing everything it can to ensure the survival of its language.
La langue de la communauté de Kahnawà:ke: The language of the Kahnawà:ke community – Kanien’kéha – is endangered. And, pandemic or not, the Kanien’kehá:ka (Mohawk) community is doing everything it can to ensure its survival.
En parlant à Steve Bonspiel, Mohawk réda: Speaking with Steve Bonspiel, the Mohawk editor-in-chief of Kahnawà:ke’s English-language newspaper The Eastern Door, it quickly becomes clear that the situation of his community’s language is not improving. Quite the opposite: Kanien’kéha is heading toward extinction. So are many of the roughly 70 other Indigenous languages spoken in Canada – two-thirds of them, to be exact. Since 1992, The Eastern Door has served the community in English, and sometimes in Kanien’kéha. But the small number of people who still speak the language, along with the high cost of translation, complicates the task.
« Dans le monde, il y a à peu près 3 500: “Worldwide, there are about 3,500 people who speak Kanien’kéha. Here in Kahnawà:ke, only a fraction of people understand it well: we’re talking about fewer than 10 per cent of residents, and it’s not getting any better,” he says in an interview.
En voyant la situation se dégrader de fa: Seeing the situation deteriorate in such a worrying way, Steve and his team decided to “get involved.” They are now about to devote one page a week of their publication, available in print and <l1>online</l1>, to common words and everyday conversations in Kanien’kéha. “The idea is that by offering these lessons, readers will make them their own and bring them into their lives, whether by collecting them or by printing them out. We know the key to learning a language is immersion.”
Si <l1>la collecte de fonds</l1> liée à: If the <l1>fundraising campaign</l1> tied to this initiative is a success – the goal is to raise $30,000 – the paper will be able to print the lessons until the end of the year, but the aim, of course, is for them to continue beyond that date.
Bien que ce genre d’activité immersive s: Although this kind of immersive activity is a step toward revitalizing his language, Steve is fully aware that an enormous amount of catching up is needed. “The devastation caused by residential schools, the Sixties Scoop and colonialism as a whole is still felt today. We were punished for speaking our language, and we were told that to succeed in life, we had to speak English or French,” he says.
La réserve de Kahnawà:ke et ses entrepre: The Kahnawà:ke reserve and its entrepreneurs already promote the Kanien’kehá:ka language in various ways, whether through translated stop signs – Testan – or simply through translated labels displayed in businesses. Still, Steve believes more initiatives like ongoing vocabulary learning are needed to ensure the language’s survival.
Malgré l’omniprésence de signes et de sy: Despite the omnipresence of signs and symbols in Kanien’kéha across the Kahnawà:ke territory, organizations on the reserve want more. “The community should have access to a live radio or TV program in its language,” suggests Lisa Phillips, executive director of the Kanien’kehá:ka Onkwawén:na Raotitióhkwa Language and Cultural Center (KORLCC). Most, if not all, of the programs broadcast by local stations CKER-FM and CKER-TV are in English.
Cependant, il existe des exceptions. En: There are exceptions, however. In addition to a weekly show on local radio, the centre produces a puppet TV show for children in Kanien’kéha: Tóta tánon Ohkwá:ri. “It’s an effective way to bring little ones together with their parents and grandparents, so they can all learn together,” explains the project’s Mohawk artistic director, Marion Delalonde. On one hand, the little ones are captivated by the funny, colourful scenes; on the other, the subjects addressed speak to a much wider audience.
Pour sensibiliser les téléspectateurs au: To raise viewers’ awareness of the challenges facing the Indigenous reserve, episodes deal with subjects such as mental health, substance abuse, diabetes and obesity. This year, Marion and her team brought in an environmental technician to help design a character who knows a lot about climate justice. “Not only do we make sure to offer content that is relevant to people here, but we also ask them to send us ideas that could become the subject of an episode, and sometimes even to take part as performer-puppeteers,” says Marion happily, stressing the show’s ability to bring people together.
L’apprentissage de la langue est aussi u: Learning the language is also a way for some people to come together, share and learn from one another. Also at KORLCC, Karonhiióstha Shea Sky, a cultural development officer, is currently developing a mentorship program in which a community member who has a strong command of the traditional language would be paired with a learner.
Karonhiióstha Shea Sky a participé au pr: Karonhiióstha Shea Sky took part in KORLCC’s Kanien’kéha immersion program. Learning her language allowed her to meet people she probably would not have met otherwise, she tells us. With her mentorship project, she hopes to strengthen this kind of connection between the different generations of her community and, ultimately, contribute to the resurgence of a proud Indigenous identity. The criminology graduate also believes these programs help prevent several social problems found on Indigenous reserves.
« L’apprentissage du kanien’kéha m’a per: “Learning Kanien’kéha allowed me to revisit my ancestors’ ways of seeing and thinking. It goes far beyond simple word-for-word translation,” she adds. For example, when a Mohawk person says Akhwá:tsire, they are talking about their family, but literally, it means “my fire.”
Les efforts déployés à l’échelle communa: Community-level efforts keep Indigenous languages alive. But what can governments do? Last fall, the Canadian government passed <l1>Bill C-91</l1>, which aims to ensure the survival of Indigenous languages. To support this commitment, the Office of the Commissioner of Indigenous Languages was created. The federal government has also allocated $333.7 million over five years for the preservation of more than 70 languages spoken by First Nations, Inuit and Métis in Canada.
Alors pourquoi les initiatives comme cel: So why do initiatives like The Eastern Door’s depend on fundraising campaigns?
Interrogé à ce sujet, le bureau de Marc: Asked about this, the office of Marc Miller, Minister of Indigenous Services, declined to give us an interview. As of publication, we had also not received answers to the questions we had sent by email.
À l’échelon provincial, les initiatives: At the provincial level, Quebec Indigenous community initiatives can obtain some funding under the Projets ponctuels autochtones program, says the press secretary for Sylvie D’Amours, the minister responsible for Indigenous Affairs. She points out that initiatives led by non-profit organizations may be eligible for the program.
« Le hic, avec le modèle actuel, c’est q: “The catch with the current model is that funds are paid out after a project is submitted, not through core funding,” says Lisa Phillips of KORLCC. “For one thing, it takes a lot of preparation time, but it also takes patience. And although the amount seems impressive, every reserve in Canada wants its share. It’s very competitive,” she says.
Malgré le financement accordé à la prése: Despite the funding granted for preserving Indigenous languages, Québec solidaire (QS) co-spokesperson Manon Massé believes the Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) is disconnected when it comes to how to go about it.
« Les actions de la CAQ ne sont pas cohé: “The CAQ’s actions are not consistent with the <l1>United Nations Declaration,</l1> nor with Bill C-91,” she says, denouncing the “colonial relationship” that party leader François Legault maintains with Indigenous peoples – whether through his endorsement of the Canadian Indigenous child protection system, deemed ineffective and harmful, through the CAQ’s injunction served on protesters at the Saint-Lambert blockade in support of the barricades erected at oil extraction sites in Wet’suwet’en, through its funding of the forestry industry and, above all, through its absence from a meeting between Quebec and the First Nations last fall (Ms. D’Amours represented the government on that occasion).
Asked about this, Mr. Legault’s office replied that he has been committed to responding to the calls to action and to justice since the Viens Commission and MMIWG reports were tabled. “The Government of Quebec has adopted an action plan for the social and cultural development of the First Nations and Inuit, in effect until 2022, which includes a component aimed at promoting Indigenous languages. Several ministries have implemented various measures under the plan aimed at promoting Indigenous languages. The work continues,” said the premier’s press secretary, Ewan Sauvé.
Alisha Tukkiapik, membre de la Commissio: Alisha Tukkiapik, a member of Québec solidaire’s Commission nationale autochtone – alongside Xavier Watso and Goulemine Cadoret – wants to say that “this is only a beginning” and that there is “a lot of work ahead.” Her language, Inuktitut, is still not recognized as a founding language of Nunavut, the territory it comes from, she illustrates. Its survival therefore rests, as almost everywhere else, solely on the will of her community. Alisha believes communities already have the solutions for maintaining their languages. “They just need to listen to us,” she says of her government.
En attendant, le succès des initiatives: In the meantime, the success of initiatives like The Eastern Door’s depends on the public. “Of course we would love to receive funding,” says Steve, noting that a member of his team is working on it. “But to date, this project relies solely on the help received from the fundraiser.”
« Chaque petite contribution compte, rap: “Every little contribution counts,” he says. “We won’t get there alone.”
